corrections.caveats: First-party book measurement: one run, online gcc 15 at -O2 (per the lead), CPU not stated; the gain is small (about 10%). Benchmark program is chapter10/chunk_sized_allocator.cpp: it prints the two timings but the repo holds no results, compiler line or CPU. The pool's three malloc'd blocks (100,000 slots each of 32, 64 and 128 bytes, about 22 MB) are allocated in the constructor outside the timed region, but their pages are first touched inside the timed chunked run. The std::vector of 300,000 (pointer, std::function) pairs is allocated in each lambda's init-capture before the clock starts and freed after it stops; filling it and the std::function type erasure are timed on both sides. The standard version runs first in the same process. The chunked allocate locks a std::mutex per call while deallocate does nothing; the book itself warns that locking strongly affects the gain and locking in deallocate would likely erase it. No memory reuse (freed slots are never handed out again; when a class fills up, requests fall through to ::operator new), so not like for like with a real allocator.

notes: Code matches the lead's description (sizes 32, 62 rounded to 64, 128; N = 100,000; dummy<30>, dummy<60>, dummy<100>). Book figures could not be checked (book not consulted per harness; wandbox permalinks not opened); kept at C per the wave12 book-record precedent.

corrections.caveats: First-party book measurement: one run on an unnamed online gcc 15 machine (per the lead), CPU not stated; flags and numbers come from the book, not the repo. The repo carries the benchmark programs in chapter10 (carnage-stdlib-version.cpp, carnage-homemade-version-meyers-singleton.cpp, carnage-homemade-version-global-singleton.cpp, carnage-homemade-version-SizeBasedArena.cpp, carnage-homemade-version-SizeBasedArena-safer.cpp) with no printed results or build lines; the record's figures cover only the stdlib, Meyers-singleton and global-singleton variants. Not like for like: the arena never reuses memory, delete does nothing, and the test is allocate-all then free-all, the best case for a bump allocator. The 0 us delete in the global-singleton version means the compiler removed the whole loop (empty deallocate, no static-local guard); the Meyers version's 638 us is mostly the per-call static-local guard check. In the Meyers-singleton version the arena's one-time malloc of 1,000,000 Orc slots (16 MB) runs inside the first timed operator new call, and the arena's pages are first touched in the timed loop on both homemade variants. The std::vector<Orc*> is reserved before timing on all variants. The arena locks a std::mutex per allocation while glibc malloc takes its single-thread fast path. Generic typed-arena speedup over malloc is well known; the evidence is a teaching example.

notes: Diffed the five carnage files: stdlib and Meyers versions differ only by the HOMEMADE_VERSION define, the global version moves the singleton to a static member. sizeof(Orc) is 16 bytes (char[4], int, double). Book figures not checked (book not consulted per harness).

corrections.caveats: The numbers are NOT from the book or its repo: the book measures no time (only code size of the same GPIO setup in HAL, LL, C and assembly on STM32F411 at -O0, not in the repo). They come from an unrelated student repo (dotsolvit/stm32f0-gpio-speed-comparison, 0 stars, no LICENSE file in its top-level listing, commits 2026-09-22 to 2026-09-24) measuring the same technique on a different chip (STM32F072 Cortex-M0, not the book's STM32F411 Cortex-M4). Its main.c loop confirms the code (HAL_GPIO_WritePin(GPIOC, GPIO_PIN_8, ...) versus GPIOC->BSRR = GPIO_BSRR_BS_8 / GPIO_BSRR_BR_8, switched by commenting; the committed main.c has the HAL block active) and its method meets tier A, so the tier is capped at B because it measures the technique on another chip rather than the book repo's code. The -O0 row (14.5x) is a debug build; use the -O2/-O3 rows (9.7x). The HAL baseline is fair on parameter checks (stm32f0xx_hal_conf.h leaves USE_FULL_ASSERT off), but the README's claim that HAL is inlined at -O2 is unlikely: the Keil project has LTO off (v6Lto 0) and HAL_GPIO_WritePin lives in a separate driver file, so each HAL write is a real call. The measured pulse width is a toggle-loop artifact: at -O2 and -O3 the BSRR pulse train is non-uniform (grouped pulses, gap every 4 cycles, author attributes it to loop unrolling and flash prefetch, unverified) and ringing is visible below 100 ns. The loop only measures two GPIO writes, not a realistic firmware workload. The book repo's own GPIO driver (Chapter7-GpioInput/Src/gpio.c) writes GPIOA->BSRR |= LED_BS5, a read-modify-write form, not the plain store that was benchmarked. A second independent data point from a tutorial page (VictorTagayun/Basic_DSMPS_Tutorial, NUCLEO-F334R8 at 72 MHz, optimization level not stated): HAL_GPIO_WritePin loop 806 kHz versus GPIOC->BSRR/BRR 2.94 MHz toggle frequency. LL is not compared in either source. Chapter 2 and 6 comparison code (HAL, LL, C, assembly) is not visible in the repo folder listings opened (Chapter1, Chapter2, Chapter7).

notes: Numbers, hardware, compiler and ratios match the benchmark README exactly; metadata (MIT, 317 stars, last commit 2025-12-15) confirmed. baseline_in_list set false: STM32 HAL is not among the filesystems-and-io baselines (POSIX read/write, mmap, io_uring); the category itself is a poor fit for a GPIO technique, consider a category override.
